results.question_title: [FEAT] Fast API Middleware in Routers

vector.answer:
The sections show FastAPI already has a mechanism for exactly the use case you describe: dependencies attached at router and application level, so shared logic like authentication or database access is written once rather than on every route.

You can pass dependencies when including a router:

    app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", tags=["admin"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={418: {"description": "I'm a teapot"}})

And you can declare global dependencies on the app itself, which are combined with the dependencies of each APIRouter:

    app = FastAPI(dependencies=[Depends(get_query_token)])

APIRouter is described as a mini FastAPI class that supports all the same options, including parameters, responses, dependencies and tags, and a router can be included in another router with router.include_router(other_router), so the shared behaviour composes down a tree.

What the sections do not cover: any middleware or extension hook on APIRouter, and any after response hook equivalent to your after_request. They document dependencies only, not a before/after request extension API.
vector.reason: Presents router- and app-level dependencies as the answer and asserts the material has no middleware hook, missing the maintainer's key point that the snippet is simply middleware, which FastAPI already documents.

graph.answer:
FastAPI already supports this, via router-level dependencies rather than an extension class.

Put the shared logic (authentication, database access) in a dependency function in its own module, then attach it to the whole router instead of to each route:

`router = APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={404: {"description": "Not found"}})`

Every path operation on that router then has that dependency evaluated before it runs, for every request. If you cannot modify the router (for example it is shared across projects), pass the same parameters when including it instead: `app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", tags=["admin"], dependencies=[Depends(get_token_header)], responses={418: {...}})`. That leaves the original router untouched. You can also set `dependencies=[...]` on the `FastAPI` app itself.

Order of execution: router dependencies first, then dependencies declared in the path operation decorator, then normal parameter dependencies. No value is passed to the path operation function for router dependencies, so they suit checks that raise `HTTPException`. `Security` dependencies with scopes work here too.

The sections do not cover an after-response hook, so I cannot speak to your `after_request` method.

results.question_title: Feature Request: Allow route return types to be FileResponse | JSONResponse

vector.answer:
The sections show two documented ways to do this today.

First, set response_model=None. This makes FastAPI skip response model generation, so you can keep any return type annotation you need without it affecting the application, which is exactly the case shown in the docs:

    @app.get("/portal", response_model=None)
    async def get_portal(teleport: bool = False) -> Response | dict:

That removes the need for the # type: ignore comments while keeping FileResponse | JSONResponse in the signature.

Second, if you do not need the union in the annotation, annotate the return as Response. FastAPI handles that automatically because the annotation is the Response class or a subclass of it, and type checkers are satisfied since the concrete response classes are subclasses of Response.

For the OpenAPI side, the docs show returning a FileResponse directly from a path operation and declaring the extra media type with the responses parameter, for example responses={200: {"content": {"image/png": {}}, "description": "Return the JSON item or an image."}}, so both outcomes are documented.

results.question_title: Unexpected Behavior with Aliased Query Parameters in FastAPI

vector.answer:
This is the intended behavior. From the alias documentation: when you declare an alias, "that alias is what will be used to find the parameter value." So alias='employee_name' makes employee_name the name FastAPI reads from the query string. emp_name is only the Python variable name that receives the value; it stops being the name clients send.

That is why /employee/?emp_name=apple falls into the else branch: nothing named employee_name was sent, the parameter takes its default of None, and `if emp_name` is false. /employee/?employee_name=apple supplies the value, so the if branch runs.

The rationale given in the docs is that the external parameter name often cannot be a Python variable name. Their example wants item-query in the URL; the closest legal Python name is item_query, so you write q: Annotated[str | None, Query(alias="item-query")] = None and the alias is what is looked up. The alias replaces the public name rather than adding a second accepted spelling.

vector.answer:

results.question_title: Continue a StreamingResponse function after client disconnect

vector.answer:
The `CancelledError` is expected. The Custom Response note on `StreamingResponse` says an async task can only be cancelled when it reaches an `await`; when the client goes away the streaming task is cancelled at your next `await`, which is why execution jumps to `except asyncio.CancelledError` rather than into your `is_disconnected()` branch.

For the actual goal (a reload picks up where the stream stopped), the documented mechanism is SSE with `Last-Event-ID`, not a hand-rolled queue in `app.state`. Attach an `id` to each event and, on reconnect, read the header and skip what was already delivered:

    @app.get("/items/stream", response_class=EventSourceResponse)
    async def stream_items(last_event_id: Annotated[int | None, Header()] = None):
        start = last_event_id + 1 if last_event_id is not None else 0
        for i, item in enumerate(items):
            if i < start:
                continue
            yield ServerSentEvent(data=item, id=str(i))

The docs also recommend declaring `response_class=` on the path operation and using `yield` there instead of returning a response object directly, because that style 'handles cancellation behind the scenes for you'.

results.question_title: Cannot use Body (pydantic schemas)  and file upload together in an API

vector.answer:
This is expected, and it is an HTTP constraint rather than a FastAPI one. The docs warn that you can declare multiple File and Form parameters in a path operation, but you cannot also declare Body fields that you expect to receive as JSON, because the request body will be encoded as multipart/form-data instead of application/json. Your create_xp: EgSchemas is a JSON body field, so a multipart request carrying the file has no JSON body for it and you get 422 Unprocessable Entity.

Send everything as form data instead, declaring the model's fields as Form parameters next to the file:

from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import FastAPI, File, Form, UploadFile

@app.post("/")
async def example(
    name: Annotated[str, Form()],
    age: Annotated[int, Form()],
    file: Annotated[UploadFile, File()],
):
    return {"message": "Success", "filename": file.filename}

The files and form fields then arrive together as form data, and you can declare some files as bytes and some as UploadFile. File() also accepts metadata such as description when used with UploadFile.
vector.reason: It identifies the multipart/form-data versus application/json conflict and gives the same File() plus Form() parameter fix as the maintainer.

results.question_title: how to add a non-blocking endpoint that calls an awaitable function but can't await it

vector.answer:
Use BackgroundTasks. Declare a background_tasks: BackgroundTasks parameter on the path operation and hand it the function plus its arguments instead of awaiting it, then return right away:

from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, FastAPI

@app.post("/deal")
async def deal(waiting: float, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    background_tasks.add_task(slow, waiting)
    return {"message": "started in the background"}

You pass the function object and its arguments, so there is no un-awaited coroutine and no RuntimeWarning. results.question_title: How does StreamingResponse work?

vector.answer:
From the sections, the documented pattern is: declare `response_class=StreamingResponse` on the path operation, then `yield` each chunk from the path operation function itself. FastAPI hands each yielded chunk to the `StreamingResponse` as is: it will not convert it to JSON, will not run it through Pydantic, and will not serialize it in any way.

Example from the docs:

    @app.get("/story/stream", response_class=StreamingResponse)
    async def stream_story() -> AsyncIterable[str]:
        for line in message.splitlines():
            yield line

The return type annotation is optional here. Because FastAPI does not serialize the data, the annotation is only for your editor and tools; it is not used by FastAPI. The docs state this leaves you with "the freedom and responsibility" to produce and encode the exact bytes you want sent.

On your second question: the sections do not mention `stream_response`, and they do not document the constructor form in your example (passing a generator to `StreamingResponse(...)` and returning it). I cannot describe the internals of how the generator is consumed from what is provided here.

graph.answer:
`StreamingResponse` takes an async generator or a normal generator/iterator (a function with `yield`) and streams the response body. Each value you yield is sent as a chunk, so your `fake_video_streamer` streams ten chunks of bytes.

One technical detail from the docs applies to your exact example: an async task can only be cancelled when it reaches an `await`. If the generator has no `await`, it cannot be cancelled properly and may keep running even after cancellation is requested. The docs version of this same example adds `await anyio.sleep(0)` after the yield to give the event loop a chance to handle cancellation. That matters more with large or infinite streams. Your code omits it.

The docs also recommend not returning `StreamingResponse` directly. Instead declare `response_class=StreamingResponse` on the path operation and use `yield` in the path operation function itself. FastAPI hands each chunk to the `StreamingResponse` as is and does not try to convert it to JSON, and this style handles cancellation for you. For JSON Lines specifically, see the Stream JSON Lines tutorial.

results.question_title: set_cookie straight up broken

vector.answer:
Not a bug. The problem is that you set the cookie on the injected `response` parameter but then return a `PlainTextResponse` directly.

The docs describe two distinct mechanisms:

1. `Response` parameter: you declare `response: Response`, set cookies on that temporary object, and then return a normal object (a dict, a model, etc.). FastAPI uses that temporary response to extract the cookies, headers, and status code and puts them into the final response it builds around your returned value.

2. Returning a `Response` directly: you create the response yourself, set the cookies on that object, and return it.

The docs warn explicitly: "if you return a response directly instead of using the `Response` parameter, FastAPI will return it directly." Your `PlainTextResponse` is returned as is, so the temporary `response` object you set the cookie on is never used, and no `Set-Cookie` header reaches the browser.

Fix it either way: build the `PlainTextResponse` first and call `set_cookie` on it before returning it, or drop the explicit response and return plain content so FastAPI merges the cookie from the `Response` parameter.

results.question_title: @app.middleware("http") wrong execution order

vector.answer:
This is by design, and it is documented. From the middleware docs:

"When you add multiple middlewares using either `@app.middleware()` decorator or `app.add_middleware()` method, each new middleware wraps the application, forming a stack. The last middleware added is the *outermost*, and the first is the *innermost*. On the request path, the *outermost* middleware runs first. On the response path, it runs last."

So in your code `test1` is added first (innermost) and `test2` second (outermost). Request order is test2 -> test1 -> route, and response order is route -> test1 -> test2. That is exactly the output you are seeing.

The docs give the same example with `add_middleware`:

    app.add_middleware(MiddlewareA)
    app.add_middleware(MiddlewareB)

    Request:  MiddlewareB -> MiddlewareA -> route
    Response: route -> MiddlewareA -> MiddlewareB

Both registration styles behave identically here, and the docs describe this stacking as what "ensures that middlewares are executed in a predictable and controllable order." If you want `test1` to run first on the request path, register it last.
vector.reason: States the maintainer's stacking rule, last added is outermost and runs first on the request path and last on the response path.

results.question_title: `Depends` does not work with `asynccontextmanager` anymore

vector.answer:
This is expected behaviour, not a bug: you should not apply the decorator yourself. The docs state that FastAPI uses `@contextlib.contextmanager` and `@contextlib.asynccontextmanager` internally for dependencies with `yield`, and say plainly that you do not have to use the decorators for FastAPI dependencies, and you should not, because FastAPI will do it for you internally. Any function that would be valid to use with those decorators is already valid as a FastAPI dependency in its undecorated form.

So drop `@asynccontextmanager` and pass the plain async generator:

    async def get_hi():
        try:
            yield 'hi'
        finally:
            print('finally')

Because you decorated it, `Depends(get_hi)` calls the decorated callable and receives the `_AsyncGeneratorContextManager` object, which is exactly what you printed.

If you have an existing context manager you want to reuse, the documented pattern is to enter it inside a dependency with `yield`, using `with` or `async with`, and yield the value from there.
vector.reason: Matches the maintainer: remove the @asynccontextmanager decorator because FastAPI wraps the plain generator itself.

graph.answer:
Drop the @asynccontextmanager decorator. FastAPI has its own handling for dependencies that yield: you write the dependency as a plain generator function and FastAPI enters and exits it for you. From 'Dependencies with yield': only the code prior to and including the yield runs before the response is created, 'The yielded value is what is injected into path operations and other dependencies', and the code following the yield runs after the response. The documented shape is your function without the decorator:

async def get_hi():
    try:
        yield 'hi'
    finally:
        print('finally')

Then hi: Annotated[str, Depends(get_hi)] receives 'hi'. You can use async or regular functions; FastAPI does the right thing with each.

With the decorator applied, get_hi is simply a callable that FastAPI calls, and what that call returns, the _AsyncGeneratorContextManager object, is what gets injected. The sections do not say whether accepting @asynccontextmanager directly is intended, so they do not settle the bug claim.

graph.answer:
That JSON is supported, but you have to tell FastAPI that `c` belongs in the body. By default, a parameter of a singular type like `int` is interpreted as a query parameter; only a parameter declared as a Pydantic model is read from the request body. So with `async def test(a: A, c: int)`, FastAPI expects `a` in the body and `c` in the query string, and your `"c"` key in the JSON is never looked at.

Use `Body` to make it another body key:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Body, FastAPI

@app.post("/test")
async def test(a: A, c: Annotated[int, Body()]):
    return {"a": a, "c": c}
```

FastAPI will then expect exactly the shape you want:

```json
{
    "a": {"b": "some string"},
    "c": 5
}
```

and it will convert, validate, and document `c` as usual.
graph.reason: Gives the maintainer's exact diagnosis and fix: c: int is a query parameter and must be annotated with Body().

```python
oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")

async def get_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    credentials_exception = HTTPException(
        status_code=status.HTTP_401_UNAUTHORIZED,
        detail="Could not validate credentials",
        headers={"WWW-Authenticate": "Bearer"},
    )
    try:
        payload = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=[ALGORITHM])
        ...
    except InvalidTokenError:
        raise credentials_exception
```

Every path operation that depends on `get_current_user` then gets interception, decoding and validation for free, and it raises HTTP 401 right away on an invalid token. Your `role` claim is just a key in the decoded `payload` dict.

```bash
uvx library-skills
```

results.question_title: How to add Custom Error that are properly converted in the OpenAPI schema? (missing `detail` prop in `response`)

vector.reason: Matches the maintainer's wrapper-model approach, declaring a model with a detail field holding the custom error model so the documented schema matches HTTPException's body.

graph.answer:
Declare a model for the whole response body, not just for the payload you put in detail.

The responses parameter takes the Pydantic model under the model key, generates its JSON Schema, and places it at content -> application/json -> schema for that status code. That schema describes the entire body. Because FastAPI's HTTPException carries your JSON-able payload in the detail field, the real body has one extra level that your model does not describe, which is exactly the mismatch you are seeing.

So wrap it:

class PlaylistNotFoundResponse(BaseModel):
    detail: HttpError_PlaylistNotFound

@app.get("/playlists/{playlist_id}", responses={404: {"model": PlaylistNotFoundResponse}})

Keep raising HTTPException as you do now, and the documented schema will match the actual JSON.

The alternative is to drop the wrapper instead of documenting it: return a JSONResponse directly with status_code=404 and your model's dump as the content, so the flat body matches the flat schema. Note that a Response returned directly is sent as is, with no model serialization, so make sure the content is valid JSON.
graph.reason: Gives the same detail-wrapper model the maintainer's generic ErrorResponse[T] provides, plus the alternative of returning a JSONResponse directly to flatten the body.
